name: Independent on Sunday cryptic crossword No 1,777

entries.clue: Fishy expression - up to no good (4)

indicators.note: UP TO gone bad, so its letters are disordered

annotation.surface: Someone pulling a sulky, guilty face while plotting mischief.
annotation.walkthrough: The pout is a fish as well as a sulky face, so 'Fishy expression' packs two readings into two words, and the anagram of UP TO confirms it.
annotation.definitionFit: A pout is both a fish and a sulky pushed-out-lips expression.

entries.clue: Hunter concealed in middle of ox-bow lake (3)

indicators.note: the answer sits inside the run of letters that follows

blocks.note: the letters straddle the end of ox-bow and the start of lake

annotation.surface: A predator lying in wait by an ox-bow lake.
annotation.walkthrough: An ox-bow lake is a curved lake left behind when a river changes course; the hyphen and space are ignored when reading across.
annotation.definitionFit: Owls are nocturnal birds of prey, so hunters.

entries.clue: Hemp wound up counterpart with tackle on the right wing (5)

indicators.note: the right-hand edge of 'tackle' is its last letter

annotation.surface: A football report: a counterpart's tackle out on the right wing.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Tackle' and 'right wing' paint a football match; here the wing is just the right-hand end of the word.
annotation.definitionFit: Twine is string made of fibres such as hemp twisted together.

entries.clue: Succeed in quiz about cancelled or difficult subjects (4,6)

indicators.note: a cancelled item is struck off the list, so the C for about is removed from the phrase

blocks.note: to score points is to succeed in a quiz

annotation.surface: A pub-quiz team doing well on the rounds nobody likes.
annotation.walkthrough: C for 'about' is circa, as in c.1850.
annotation.definitionFit: Sore points are topics that touch a nerve, difficult to raise.

entries.clue: How walks up Kilimanjaro and fun runs are backed, or by whom? (7)

annotation.definition: How walks up Kilimanjaro and fun runs are backed, or by whom?

blocks.clueFragment: How walks up Kilimanjaro and fun runs are backed
blocks.note: the verb: charity challenges are funded by people pledging money per mile, so they are backed this way
the noun: the person who pledges the money

annotation.surface: Wondering how charity challenges get their funding.
annotation.walkthrough: The answer covers both halves: charity walks are backed by sponsorship (how) and by a sponsor (who).
annotation.definitionFit: A sponsor pays out for someone else's charity walk or run, and to sponsor is to fund it.

entries.clue: Macabre effect of 22D 13A is as yet unknown (7,2,2,4)

blocks.note: a body in a see-through casket is on display: literally what is left, there to be looked at
the everyday idiom for an outcome nobody can predict yet

annotation.surface: Speculating about a gruesome display whose outcome is still unknown.
annotation.walkthrough: 22D and 13A together make GLASS COFFIN, as in Snow White; a body in one is literally remains to be seen.
annotation.definitionFit: One sense is the idiom for an undecided outcome; the other is a literal reading, a corpse's remains visible through glass.

entries.clue: Bird chewed a pencil (7)

indicators.note: chewed things are mangled out of shape

annotation.surface: A bird gnawing on a pencil.
annotation.walkthrough: A short, straightforward anagram with the definition first.
annotation.definitionFit: A pelican is a large water bird with a throat pouch.

entries.clue: Unusually fine story that’s hard to describe (9)

indicators.note: FINE appears in an unusual order

annotation.surface: Praising a remarkably good tale that defies description.
annotation.walkthrough: Only the first word is scrambled; FABLE goes in as it is.
annotation.definitionFit: Ineffable means too great to be expressed in words.

entries.clue: London and SE might be OK, somehow (3,3,5)

indicators.note: the letters are rearranged in some way

annotation.surface: A shrug about London and the South East being fine, more or less.
annotation.walkthrough: SE looks like the South East, but it is just two letters of the fodder.
annotation.definitionFit: The Big Smoke is an old nickname for London, from its coal-smoke fogs.

entries.clue: Cause of extreme weather faked online (2,4)

indicators.note: something faked is made up, re-formed

annotation.surface: Fake news on the internet about the cause of freak weather.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface reads as a comment on misinformation; 'faked' is the only instruction.
annotation.definitionFit: El Niño is the Pacific warming pattern that disrupts weather worldwide.

entries.clue: Graduate student briefly put right about Sartre's Nausea (3,2,3)

indicators.note: the last letter of REMEDY is cut
the shortened word is turned round

blocks.note: REMEDY without its Y, then turned round

annotation.surface: A postgraduate correcting a view of Sartre's novel.
annotation.walkthrough: Sartre's novel La Nausée is French, and 'Sartre's' signals a French answer: mal de mer is French for seasickness. L = learner, as on a British learner-driver plate.
annotation.definitionFit: Mal de mer is seasickness, a kind of nausea, in French.

entries.clue: Sporting footwear with a snappy outfit, both trimmed (5,3)

indicators.note: TERSE and KIT each lose their last letter

annotation.surface: Sports shoes worn with a smart outfit, both cut short.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Snappy outfit' reads as a stylish suit, but it is two words each doing its own job: terse and kit.
annotation.definitionFit: A water ski is worn on the feet for a sport, so a jokey piece of sporting footwear.

entries.clue: Boundless energy from a cat with one special ability - absorbing carbon! (6,5)

indicators.note: the string built so far takes C inside it

blocks.note: a tom is a male cat
a power, as a superhero has

annotation.surface: A superhero cat that soaks up carbon for limitless energy.
annotation.walkthrough: C goes between I and POWER. 'Boundless' is fair because nuclear power was once promised as near-limitless.
annotation.definitionFit: Atomic power is energy from nuclear reactions, once sold as practically boundless.

entries.clue: Acrostic of "find accommodating receptacle to entomb dead" (6)

indicators.note: the opening words hold the answer inside them

blocks.note: the letters run from the tail of acrostic, through of, into the start of find

annotation.surface: A puzzle instruction to make an acrostic from a phrase about burial.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Acrostic' begs you to take first letters, which spell nothing useful; the word itself holds the answer's opening letter.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the box a body is buried in, described at length to hide the word.

entries.clue: School rebuffed pupil’s denial, employing a process for detecting plagiarism (10)

indicators.note: the denial is pushed back, turned round
to employ is to take on, so COMP takes on the A as its next piece

annotation.surface: A school dismissing a pupil's protest after catching them copying.
annotation.walkthrough: A comp is a British state comprehensive school; 'No, sir' is how a pupil denies something to a male teacher.
annotation.definitionFit: Comparing texts side by side is how plagiarism is caught.

entries.clue: Post Office is working to shut up malicious writer (6,3)

blocks.note: to pen is to shut up, enclose

annotation.surface: The Post Office working to silence someone sending nasty letters.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Shut up' reads as silencing; it means enclosing, as sheep are penned.
annotation.definitionFit: A poison pen is the anonymous author of spiteful letters.

entries.clue: Play outside transport terminal in Chiswick (4)

indicators.note: the terminal letter of Chiswick

annotation.surface: Someone playing music outside a bus station in Chiswick.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Transport terminal' reads as a bus station; it splits into BUS and the terminal letter. Chiswick is a district of west London.
annotation.definitionFit: To busk is to perform music in the street for money.

entries.clue: Antipodean’s vital amber liquid, we hear (4)

indicators.note: the answer is said, not spelt, like the words

blocks.note: key = vital, wee = urine, an amber liquid

annotation.surface: An Australian or New Zealander's essential cold beer.
annotation.walkthrough: Amber liquid looks like lager, which suits an Antipodean; here it is urine, 'wee' in British slang.
annotation.definitionFit: Kiwi is the everyday name for a New Zealander, an Antipodean.

entries.clue: Owner's organised report about dog permit oddly ignored (10)

indicators.note: organised things have been put into a new order, so the letters of report are rearranged
the rearranged letters go around the others
the odd letters of dog permit are dropped

annotation.surface: A dog owner's report on a missed licence.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Owner's' is the definition plus 's for 'is'. 'Dog' looks like the animal that needs the permit, but it is only letters to thin out.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the proprietor of a shop or hotel is its legal owner.

entries.clue: Snooker player Hendry’s last cup, perhaps (7)

indicators.note: the final letter of Hendry

annotation.surface: A snooker champion's last trophy.
annotation.walkthrough: Stephen Hendry was a snooker champion, and 'cup' looks like his trophy; it is a china cup, an example of pottery. 'Perhaps' marks the example.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: a cup is one kind of pottery, which 'perhaps' flags.

entries.clue: Welsh dish provided in bloody small portion (7)

blocks.note: a bit is a small portion

annotation.surface: A restaurant serving a Welsh dish in a stingy helping.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Bloody' reads as the British intensifier; it describes undercooked meat. Welsh rarebit is cheese on toast.
annotation.definitionFit: Welsh rarebit is a savoury cheese sauce on toast.

entries.clue: Don't take part in operation against ticket seller (3,3)

annotation.surface: Refusing to join a sting against a ticket seller.
annotation.walkthrough: A tout is someone reselling tickets at inflated prices outside a venue.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym for declining to participate, as when opting out of a scheme.

entries.clue: Ex-PM brewing lager with last vestiges of her late barley (4,4)

indicators.note: the letters are stirred together
the final letters of the following words

blocks.clueFragment: last vestiges of her late barley
blocks.note: last letters of heR, latE, barleY

annotation.surface: A former prime minister brewing her own beer.
annotation.walkthrough: Earl Grey was Prime Minister in the 1830s, and the tea named after him is brewed too. 'Her' makes you picture a woman PM.
annotation.definitionFit: Charles, the second Earl Grey, was British Prime Minister 1830-34.

entries.clue: It's clear from the outset - girls love anagrams and silly spoonerisms ... (5)

indicators.note: the words' opening letters

blocks.note: first letters of Girls Love Anagrams

annotation.surface: Declaring that girls obviously love wordplay, continued in the next clue.
annotation.walkthrough: 'And' is left out of the first letters. The ellipsis runs on to 25D.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by description: transparency is glass's defining property, and 'It' stands for the answer.

entries.clue: Maybe Simon and Garfunkel's Sound of Silence toasted thus? (3-5)

indicators.note: the sound of a phrase, not its spelling, is what counts

blocks.note: a toast begins 'To ...!', raising a glass to something
peace = silence, as in peace and quiet

annotation.surface: Wondering whether a famous duo's song was once raised in a toast.
annotation.walkthrough: The Sound of Silence is a Simon and Garfunkel song, so the title reads as one unit; split it after 'Sound of'. A duo is a two-piece band, and 'Maybe' marks it as one example.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: a duo is a two-piece act, and Simon and Garfunkel are a famous duo.

entries.clue: Born horny? This might calm one down (6)

annotation.surface: A remedy for someone overexcited.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface hints a nightcap cools ardour; brandy is the traditional drink for shock.
annotation.definitionFit: Brandy is the traditional drink to steady someone's nerves.

entries.clue: ... like mine (3)

blocks.note: slang verb from jazz talk: to appreciate, to be into something
verb: to excavate, to tunnel into the ground

annotation.surface: Continuing 22D: silly spoonerisms, like the setter's own.
annotation.walkthrough: The ellipsis joins this to 22D, so 'mine' seems to mean the setter's own spoonerisms. It is two verbs: to dig something is to like it, and to dig is to mine.
annotation.definitionFit: Two verb senses: dig as enjoy, from jazz slang, and dig as excavate.

entries.clue: "Poorly managed reef, greater action necessary" - Kenyan oceanologist taking sides (6,4)

indicators.note: take each word's two edge letters

annotation.surface: A Kenyan marine scientist warning that a coral reef is being mismanaged.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is about coral; the reef is a reef knot, and a granny knot is the reef knot tied wrongly.
annotation.definitionFit: A granny knot is a botched reef knot, crossed the wrong way.

entries.clue: Afghans regularly overthrown in epic story (4)

indicators.note: at regular intervals, so every other letter is taken
the result is toppled, turned back

blocks.note: A f G h A n S

annotation.surface: Afghan rulers toppled again and again in a long historical tale.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Overthrown' suits the political surface; here it only turns the letters round.
annotation.definitionFit: A saga is a long heroic narrative, an epic.
